items.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning (PPFL) Testbed and Curated Dataset
items.authors: NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence
items.summary: NCCoE released software for comparing centralised and federated learning, with optional differential privacy, alongside a curated soybean genomic dataset.
items.relevance: A practical resource for studying privacy and model-performance trade-offs when organisations cannot pool sensitive data. Its initial benchmark concerns genomics; applications to behavioural security would need separate evaluation.

items.title: Design Tenets for Agent Identity Management Systems
items.authors: Harold Booth, Bill Fisher, Ryan Galluzzo and Tom Clancy
items.summary: NIST outlines ten initial design principles for agent identity and access, including distinct identities, constrained delegation, short-lived permissions and human review. This is a project blog discussion, not a final standard.
items.relevance: Useful for examining how automated actions can be traced to their originator and how access can be revoked when behaviour changes. It also separates permission enforcement from an agent's reasoning.

items.title: Explainable multi-modal unsupervised learning for insider threat detection in enterprise environments
items.authors: Neda Baghalizadeh Moghadam, Frédéric Cuppens and Nora Boulahia-Cuppens
items.venue: Journal of Information Security and Applications, volume 102, article 104581
items.summary: An unsupervised framework combines detectors for daily user activity, calibrates anomaly scores and supplies feature explanations with behavioural summaries. The study evaluates implementations on anonymised enterprise logs and CERT r4.2.
items.relevance: Useful for distinguishing operational anomaly screening from validated threat detection: the enterprise logs lack reliable insider-threat labels, so they cannot establish detection accuracy.

items.title: Grounded theory insights into human insider threats: a qualitative study of expert perceptions
items.authors: Marcus L. Green, Priya D. Dozier and Eric Owusu
items.venue: Frontiers in Computer Science, volume 8, article 1854879
items.summary: Interviews with 15 cybersecurity professionals inform a framework connecting insider risk with employee behaviour, organisational culture, training and access controls.
items.relevance: Adds human and organisational context to behavioural detection research. The small, purposively selected expert sample and absence of interviews with offenders limit generalisation.

items.title: Counterfactual Routine Deviation: Personalised Behavioural Modelling for Insider Threat Detection
items.authors: Christian Bowie, Hadi Larijani and Ayyaz Qureshi
items.summary: A published study compares deviations from each user's historical routine with peer-based behavioural baselines using CERT r6.2. Its evaluation includes a later time period and users withheld from model fitting.
items.relevance: Useful for separating ranking performance from practical alert quality: the study reports low precision and weak generalisation to unseen users, motivating independent validation.

items.title: Towards trustworthy cybersecurity: Reclassifying insider threat detection using SHAP
items.authors: Raddad Faqihi, Priyadarsi Nanda, Manoranjan Mohanty, Saleh Alqahtani and Bashair Alrashed
items.venue: Future Generation Computer Systems, volume 183, article 108543
items.summary: A study combining SHAP feature attributions with security-domain knowledge to support analyst-guided reclassification of insider-threat predictions. The reported evaluation uses CMU CERT data.
items.relevance: Connects explanation assessment with analyst judgement. Its CERT-based findings are a useful prompt for testing explanation quality and transfer beyond a single benchmark.

items.title: A session-based insider threat detection approach leveraging the CERT and SPEDIA datasets
items.authors: Alberto Mateo Muñoz, Xavier Larriva-Novo, Carmen Sánchez-Zas, Manuel Alvarez-Campana and Victor A. Villagra
items.venue: Machine Learning with Applications, volume 25, article 100946
items.summary: A study that groups activity logs into sessions represented by 36 features, then evaluates supervised and unsupervised detection methods on CERT r4.2 and SPEDIA.
items.relevance: Useful for examining how session boundaries and feature construction affect evaluation. SPEDIA includes CERT-derived events, so the subsets used matter when interpreting cross-dataset evidence.

items.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
items.summary: A study of how to evaluate saliency methods, showing why visually convincing explanations alone are insufficient evidence of reliability.
items.relevance: A starting point for designing checks of whether an explanation depends on what a model has learned.
